title: Safety in Transportation

lessons.title: Recognize transport risk
lessons.question: Why does reaction time matter before braking begins?
ideas: A road collision can cause physical and emotional harm. Reaction time is the time between noticing a hazard and beginning a response. During that interval, a moving vehicle continues to travel.

Distraction and fatigue can delay detection and response. The distance travelled before braking depends on speed and reaction time. This is a physics model, not a substitute for current driving instruction.
lessons.model: At 20 m/s, a vehicle covers 20 m during a one-second reaction interval before braking starts. If reaction takes two seconds under the same simplified conditions, that distance doubles.
lessons.check: At 20 m/s, how far does a vehicle travel in 2 s before braking?
lessons.writing: Explain why a driver can collide with a hazard even when the brakes work correctly.

lessons.title: Explain impairment and protection
lessons.question: How can several safety layers reduce harm?
ideas: Impairment changes the ability to notice, judge and respond to hazards. The source workbook includes old BAC tables and legal questions; those values are historical course material and must not be used as current driving limits.
Vehicle features, safer roads, restraint use and attentive decisions form layers of protection. A layer may reduce risk or injury but cannot eliminate every collision.
lessons.model: A driver with a seat belt still needs attention and space to stop. The belt reduces injury during a collision; it does not shorten the reaction interval before braking.
lessons.check: What is the best description of a seat belt?
options: A restraint that can reduce injury in a collision
A device that makes reaction time zero
Proof that any driving condition is safe
lessons.writing: Pick a road scenario and explain how one prevention action and one injury-reduction feature work at different stages.

lessons.title: Calculate and graph speed
lessons.question: What does the slope of a distance–time graph tell us?
ideas: Average speed is distance divided by elapsed time. Keep units consistent: kilometres per hour and metres per second describe the same kind of rate using different units.

On a distance–time graph, time belongs on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis. The slope is change in distance divided by change in time. A horizontal segment means no change in distance.
lessons.model: A trip covers 120 km in 2 h, so average speed is 60 km/h. On a graph, points (0 h, 0 km) and (2 h, 120 km) give the same slope: 120 ÷ 2 = 60 km/h.
lessons.check: A line rises 30 m in 5 s. What speed does its slope represent?
lessons.writing: Sketch a distance–time graph for moving, stopping, then moving again. Label both axes and explain each segment.

lessons.title: Connect speed and stopping distance
lessons.question: Why does doubling speed change more than the time available?
ideas: Stopping distance includes distance travelled during reaction and distance travelled while braking. Higher speed increases the distance covered each second before braking begins.
Braking distance also depends on road and tire conditions. The textbook’s sample values illustrate a relationship; real stopping distances vary, so use current local driving guidance for decisions.
lessons.model: At 15 m/s with a 1 s reaction interval, reaction distance is 15 m. At 30 m/s with the same interval, it is 30 m before braking. The comparison isolates reaction distance only.
lessons.check: Which part of stopping distance occurs before the brake is applied?
lessons.writing: Explain how speed and a slippery road change different parts of stopping distance.

lessons.title: Calculate momentum
lessons.question: How do mass and speed affect a moving object?
ideas: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity. In a straight-line model, direction matters: opposite directions can be represented with opposite signs.
Doubling mass while keeping velocity fixed doubles momentum. Doubling velocity while keeping mass fixed also doubles momentum. The units must match the formula being used.
lessons.model: A 750 kg car moving at 20 m/s has momentum 15,000 kg·m/s. The same car at 40 m/s has 30,000 kg·m/s.
lessons.check: A 1000 kg vehicle moves at 10 m/s. What is its momentum?
lessons.writing: Calculate momentum for two vehicles with different masses and speeds. Explain which has more and why.

lessons.title: Relate impulse, force and collision
lessons.question: How does a longer stopping time affect the force?
ideas: Impulse is change in momentum. Average force multiplied by the time it acts gives the impulse. For the same momentum change, spreading the change over more time reduces average force.
Momentum is conserved for a defined system when external effects are negligible. In real collisions, energy can move into deformation, heat and sound, so do not assume kinetic energy is conserved.
lessons.model: If a momentum change of 1000 kg·m/s occurs over 0.1 s, average force magnitude is 10,000 N. Over 1 s, it is 1000 N. The model holds the momentum change fixed.
lessons.check: For the same momentum change, what happens when stopping time increases?
lessons.writing: Use a crumple zone or padded landing to explain impulse, stopping time and force.

lessons.title: Compare vehicle and road safety designs
lessons.question: How does a design reduce injury without preventing every crash?
ideas: Crumple zones deform to lengthen the time of a collision. Restraints help prevent occupants from continuing forward unprotected. Mirrors and lights support operation before a collision.
Road features such as barriers or crash cushions can redirect or absorb some collision energy. Evaluate a feature by the hazard it addresses, the mechanism and any limitations.
lessons.model: A crumple zone and a seat belt act together: the structure deforms and the belt restrains the occupant. Neither means a collision has no force or consequence.
lessons.check: Which feature works mainly by increasing collision time through controlled deformation?
lessons.writing: Choose two safety features from different categories and explain the physical mechanism of each.

lessons.title: Evaluate restraints and changing designs
lessons.question: Why must a restraint match the person and situation?
ideas: Seat belts, child restraints and air bags are designed to manage occupant motion in a collision. Their effectiveness depends on correct use and the design context.

The textbook describes historical designs. For real travel decisions, follow current manufacturer instructions and local safety requirements rather than treating the old course pages as current rules.
lessons.model: An air bag is a supplemental system. It does not replace the seat belt. A suitable child restraint must be chosen and installed according to current instructions for the child and vehicle.
lessons.check: What is the best description of an air bag?
options: A supplemental restraint used with other protections
A replacement for every seat belt
A device that removes all momentum
lessons.writing: Explain why a safety feature should be assessed as part of a system rather than in isolation.

sourceType: Brightspace textbook and workbook; newly authored online explanations and formative checks

glossary.reaction time: Time between noticing a hazard and beginning a response.
glossary.distraction: Attention drawn away from a task or hazard.
glossary.fatigue: Tiredness that can reduce alertness and performance.
glossary.risk: The chance and possible consequence of harm in a situation.
glossary.impairment: Reduced ability to perceive, judge or respond effectively.
glossary.BAC: Blood alcohol concentration, a measure of alcohol in the blood.
glossary.restraint: A device that helps limit occupant motion during a collision.
glossary.road safety: Design and behaviour intended to reduce road crashes and harm.
glossary.distance: The amount of space travelled or separation between positions.
glossary.speed: Distance travelled per unit of time.
glossary.slope: Change in the vertical graph value divided by change in the horizontal value.
glossary.reaction distance: Distance a vehicle travels before braking begins.
glossary.braking distance: Distance travelled while brakes slow the vehicle.
glossary.following distance: Space maintained between one vehicle and the vehicle ahead.
glossary.momentum: Mass multiplied by velocity, including direction.
glossary.mass: A measure of the amount of matter in an object.
glossary.friction: A force that opposes relative motion between contacting surfaces.
glossary.impulse: Change in momentum produced by a force acting over time.
glossary.force: A push or pull that can change motion.
glossary.collision: An event in which objects exert forces on one another during contact.
glossary.conservation of momentum: Total momentum of an isolated system remains the same.
glossary.crumple zone: A vehicle structure designed to deform and extend collision time.
glossary.road feature: A part of road design intended to guide traffic or reduce harm.
glossary.crash cushion: A road device designed to absorb energy in certain impacts.
glossary.seat belt: A restraint that helps keep an occupant positioned during a collision.
glossary.child restraint: A seat or system designed to restrain a child in a vehicle.
glossary.air bag: A supplemental restraint that inflates during certain collisions.
glossary.safety system: A group of features and practices working together to reduce harm.
